Man shot by ICE officer is detained in Texas with a bullet still in his back, attorney says
sources.text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A Venezuelan man shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer was in custody Monday at an ICE detention center in Texas after he was released from a hospital with a bullet still lodged in his back, the man's attorney said.
Speaking by phone during a news conference, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez said doctors didn’t remove the bullet because it’s near his spine. He said ICE pressed for him to be released quickly from the hospital so it could move him to a detention center. He said he had received no pain medication or treatment there, and had slept on the floor, before eventually being given a “pill” by a nurse on Monday.
Perez, 28, was making a DoorDash delivery in Austin on Sunday when his car was “sideswiped” twice by ICE officers in an unmarked truck, immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told reporters Monday. He was taken to a hospital, she said, but was released later Sunday into ICE custody with the bullet still inside him.
Perez said ICE officers didn’t ask him to stop or turn on any flashing lights until after they had sideswiped him. He said he did a U-turn and was trying to park when the officers rammed his car and shot him in the back of the neck.
“I am not doing well due to the gunshot wound, and I have not received the medical attention that I require,” Perez said, speaking in Spanish over the phone as a member of his attorney's staff translated during the news conference.
Perez was being detained at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, about 130 miles (209 kilometers) southwest of Austin, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. She said Perez told her in a prior phone call that he was being interrogated.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has released little information and has not said what prompted the shooting. In a statement early Monday, the department said it was investigating the shooting of a Venezuelan man in the U.S. illegally who “had a final order of removal.”
Homeland Security did not immediately respond to email messages seeking further comment on the shooting.
Perez entered the U.S. legally in 2024 after using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that set up appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day in office.
Perez's attorneys said he was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. She said a judge issued a deportation order for Perez after he missed a hearing in immigration court because the hearing notice was sent to a former address.
“Not that being out of status would justify any of this at all,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said of the shooting in a social media post.
The shooting occurred amid a surge in ICE enforcement across the U.S. during Trump's second term. During the summer, it reported more than 50,000 monthly arrests in July and August — a first for the agency.
Immigration officers have come under intense scrutiny amid a series of shootings during the crackdown. At least four people have been fatally shot by federal officers during immigration enforcement operations this year.
Local advocates, leaders of the civil rights group the League of United Latin American Citizens and two Democratic congressmen who represent parts of Austin called during the news conference for the creation of an independent body to review use-of-force incidents by ICE and refer suspected crimes to prosecutors.
They also urged Congress to ban ICE officers from making traffic stops, saying the officers are undertrained and too quick to resort to violence.
Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, has said he wants local police to have a role in investigating the shooting. Watson said it wouldn’t be appropriate for ICE to investigate on its own.
The area beneath an overpass where a large crowd of protesters had gathered Sunday near the shooting scene was quiet Monday. Trash-filled plastic bags were left below concrete pylons marked with anti-ICE graffiti.
Amid discarded police tape, people left candles, flowers and a sign that read “Justice for Wilber.”
Associated Press journalist Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed.

sources.news_title: ICE Shoots Venezuelan Man With Removal Order in Austin
sources.text:
An ICE officer shot a 28-year-old Venezuelan man during an enforcement operation in Austin, Texas, and the man had entered the country during the Biden administration and already had a judge's order sending him home.
The shooting happened on the afternoon of September 20 on Austin's north side, under a highway overpass, when Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents moved to arrest Wilber Rafael Garces Perez during what the agency called a targeted law enforcement operation. Garces Perez, who had a final order of removal issued by an immigration judge, attempted to flee, triggering a brief foot pursuit that ended when an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer fired several shots, DHS officials told Breitbart Texas. At least one round struck Garces Perez in the back of the neck.
He was transported to a local trauma center in serious but stable condition, treated, and later released, with the bullet still lodged near his spine. Doctors determined it was too risky to extract. ICE then transferred him to a detention facility in Pearsall, Texas, roughly 160 miles southwest of Austin, where he remains in custody.
The case sits at the intersection of two facts that do not easily resolve. DHS officials said Garces Perez was an illegal immigrant with a final order of removal, the legal endpoint that means an immigration judge reviewed his case and ordered him out of the country. That order made him a priority target for ICE enforcement.
But the Associated Press reported that Garces Perez initially entered the United States in 2024 through the CBP One program, the Biden-era app-based system that allowed migrants to schedule appointments at ports of entry, and that he held a valid work permit at the time of the shooting. His immigration attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, told the AP he was making a DoorDash delivery when ICE agents approached his vehicle.
How a man who entered through a lawful parole channel wound up with a final removal order is not explained in any available account. The gap matters. CBP One admissions were not border-jumping; they were appointments approved by the federal government under Biden administration policy. If Garces Perez entered through that program and later fell out of status, or if an immigration judge found his claim meritless, the removal order is the system working as designed. If the order was issued in error or is under appeal, the calculus changes. Neither DHS nor ICE has publicly clarified the sequence.
Lincoln-Goldfinch, the attorney, told reporters she and Garces Perez's wife had been blocked from seeing him and did not know his location after the transfer.
Bystander footage aired by Fox News showed the pursuit and shooting. The video showed an ICE officer approach a vehicle as the driver attempted to flee, followed by what appeared to be several gunshots. The passenger side of the vehicle sustained visible damage. DHS has not confirmed how many rounds the officer fired or how many struck Garces Perez.
An unnamed ICE official told reporters the agency is still deploying its newly funded body camera devices. Whether the officer involved was wearing one at the time is unclear, photos from the immediate aftermath suggest he was not, though that has not been officially confirmed.
ICE's Homeland Security Investigations division and the FBI are jointly leading the investigation into the shooting. Austin police are not running the probe, but the city's police chief weighed in publicly.
Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said the city deserved transparency:
"The city of Austin deserves answers. We're going to get all those questions answered, and we'll be as transparent as we can be."
Shortly after the shooting, protesters arrived at the scene carrying pre-printed anti-ICE signs. The New York Post reported the shooting triggered angry demonstrations near the overpass. How many protesters were arrested, if any, remains unclear. Who organized the rapid response and distributed the printed signs has not been reported.
Austin Mayor Kirk Watson did not hold back:
"I'm very angry about this. [But] I'm not surprised at all. It's happened in other cities with the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days and the chaos that we see it performing and fomenting."
Watson's framing, that ICE itself is "fomenting chaos", reflects a posture common among Democratic municipal leaders who have resisted federal immigration enforcement. It does not address the fact that Garces Perez had a final removal order, meaning a federal judge had already determined he had no legal right to remain in the country. Officers enforcing that order were doing what the law requires.
From the Pearsall detention center, Garces Perez spoke to reporters in Spanish by phone. He described his condition plainly:
"I am not doing well due to the gunshot wound, and I have not received the medical attention that I require."
A bullet near the spine is not a minor wound. Whether ICE's detention medical staff can provide the level of care his injury demands is a legitimate question, one that federal courts have addressed repeatedly in cases involving detained individuals with serious medical needs. If ICE is holding a man with a bullet lodged against his spinal column and providing inadequate treatment, that is a problem regardless of his immigration status.
His attorney acknowledged his immigration status had lapsed but pushed back on the idea that it justified the shooting. "Not that being out of status would justify any of this at all," Lincoln-Goldfinch told the AP.
The Austin incident is not isolated. The New York Post noted it is part of a broader pattern of ICE-involved shootings in 2026, including two fatal shootings, one in Houston and one in Maine. Civil rights organizations and some local officials have called for independent oversight of ICE use-of-force incidents, a demand that has gained traction as enforcement operations have expanded.
ICE's expanded enforcement posture is a direct policy choice, one this publication has supported as a necessary correction after years of deliberate non-enforcement. But expanded authority demands expanded accountability. Body cameras exist precisely for moments like this. If ICE is conducting armed arrest operations in American neighborhoods and its officers are not yet equipped with functioning body cameras, the agency is operating without the basic transparency tool that every local police department in the country now takes for granted.
The FBI and HSI investigation will determine whether the officer's use of force was justified. The facts known so far, a man with a removal order who fled from agents, describe a situation where force may have been warranted. But "may have been warranted" is not the same as "was warranted," and the public has seen no body camera footage, no detailed use-of-force report, and no official account of what the officer observed that prompted him to fire at a man who, by at least one account, was delivering food.
Strip away the shooting and the protests, and the underlying failure is straightforward. The Biden administration created CBP One as a mechanism to process migrants at the border in an orderly fashion. Garces Perez used that program to enter in 2024. He received a work permit. He was, by the federal government's own determination, authorized to be here.
Then an immigration judge ordered him removed. The system that let him in decided he had to leave. He did not leave. ICE came to enforce the order. He ran. An officer fired.
Every step in that chain traces back to a border policy that processed people into the country without the institutional capacity to track them, adjudicate their cases promptly, or ensure compliance with removal orders. The Biden administration admitted hundreds of thousands of people through parole programs and app-based scheduling. When those cases resolved against the applicants, enforcement fell to ICE officers making armed approaches on city streets, exactly the kind of confrontation that a functioning immigration system is supposed to prevent.
Enforcing removal orders is not optional. It is what the law demands. But the conditions that put an ICE agent and a DoorDash driver on a collision course under an Austin overpass were years in the making, and the people who built those conditions are nowhere near the scene.

sources.news_title: Migrant shot by ICE in Texas said he tried to pull over
sources.text:
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez’s wife told him to stay home on Sunday and spend time with her. But he wanted to work and earn some money as a DoorDash food delivery driver. So he left.
At 12:30 p.m. the 28-year-old immigrant from Venezuela called his wife, “shouting that he had been shot and he was in pain, and then the call cut off,” his immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said Monday at a news conference a day after the shooting in North Austin.
Garces Perez, who called into the news conference, said an unmarked SUV sideswiped him twice before he realized that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were trying to pull him over. He said he did a U-turn under a freeway underpass when the SUV struck his blue Toyota Camry. That’s when the SUVs turned on their blue-and-red lights and sirens, he said.
He asked the agents if he could stop somewhere safer than in traffic under the freeway. He said an agent told him no, then he felt one shot to his back.
He was transported to Dell Seton Medical Center, where staff told him they weren’t going to remove the bullet because it was too close to his spine, Garces Perez said in the call from the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, about a two hour drive south of Austin.
He said that at 4 a.m. he was transferred to a temporary processing center, where he slept on the concrete floor of a cell.
“I’m not doing very well,” he said. “I have not received the medical attention that I require.”
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Garces Perez’s account of what happened prior to the shooting and his complaint about inadequate medical care.
It’s the third time ICE officers have shot a person in Texas since President Donald Trump returned to the White House. The other two shootings — of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston in July and Ruben Ray Martinez in March 2025 in South Padre Island — were fatal.
The Trump administration has prioritized immigration enforcement, vowing to conduct the largest deportation in the country’s history. Under his administration, ICE has increased street arrests, looking for immigrants — even those who entered the country legally — to detain and deport.
“We are fed up with ICE and DHS telling us lies about what has happened in these incidents where people are being murdered and shot,” said Lincoln-Goldfinch, an Austin-based immigration attorney.
In previous ICE shootings, DHS has released preliminary information that was later contradicted by video footage or witness statements. For example, In Salgado Araujo’s case, DHS initially said that he tried to ram ICE vehicles. But the other three men in the van later said Salgado Araujo never tried to hit the officers after and instead, ICE vehicles struck them from behind and the side before one of the agents fired, striking Salgado Araujo in the stomach.
After immigration agents in January fatally shot 37-year-old Renée Good and 37-year-old Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during separate protests against immigration enforcement operations, DHS claimed Good tried to run over ICE agents and that Pretti had tried to harm immigration agents. But video footage called those accounts into question.
The New York Times reported that ICE agents were in the North Austin area running background checks on motorists’ license plates when they found Garces Perez, who had a deportation order on file. DHS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
According to a Texas Tribune analysis of federal government data as of early August, ICE’s San Antonio area of responsibility, which includes Austin, has seen one of the largest shifts toward street arrests — ranking third among the nation’s 25 areas of responsibility.
Garces Perez entered the U.S. two years ago using the CBP One cellphone application, which the Biden administration set up to allow some immigrants make appointments with immigration agents at a port of entry, his lawyer said. After being processed by immigration officials, he was allowed to enter the U.S. and then applied for asylum, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. He later received a work permit.
After settling in Austin, he updated his home address with the immigration court, his lawyer said. But the court sent a notice of his court hearing to a previous address, so Garces Perez didn’t know he had missed a court appearance, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. As a result, the immigration judge issued a deportation order, which he was not notified about, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
“I’ve been an immigration lawyer for 20 years, doing removal defense cases, like thousands of cases in the immigration court system. This is a very common outcome that the immigration court does not properly update people’s addresses,” she said. “The person doesn’t arrive, and they order them deported in absentia. I would say, maybe daily in my law practice, we see this happen.”
There were nearly 90,300 removal orders in absentia for asylum applicants as of the third quarter of fiscal year 2026, continuing the sharp rise that started since Trump’s return to office, according to federal data. Along with common reasons such as notices being sent to the wrong address, ICE also started arresting people at immigration courts last year, creating a chilling effect that has led some immigrants to skip their hearings out of fear of being detained.
During the Biden administration, hundreds of thousands of immigrants arrived at the border, many of them Venezuelans seeking political asylum. In the two years that CBP One was in use, 936,500 people made appointments and legally crossed the border, with the top nationalities being Venezuelan, Cuban and Mexican.
But on Trump’s first day back in the White House, he ended the use of CBP One, revoked the parole status of everyone who entered using the application and canceled all scheduled appointments.
Advocacy groups have sued the Trump administration over the moves, arguing that the White House didn’t properly cancel the programs and that the Biden administration had the legal right to parole immigrants into the country under immigration law. The lawsuits are pending.
Kristin Etter, another Austin immigration attorney representing Garces Perez, filed a request for his release and to block his deportation in a federal court in San Antonio on Monday.
Etter wrote in the court documents that her client is not disputing the final removal order but wants a chance to apply for a U-visa, a type of immigration status for victims and witnesses of a crime. Etter also wrote that because the shooting is now being investigated as a potential crime, he has the right to apply for a U visa.
“The current administration has demonstrated a pattern of accelerating immigration enforcement against individuals connected to incidents involving federal immigration officers, raising a substantial and immediate concern that (the federal government) will attempt to remove (Garces Perez) before he has an opportunity to pursue U nonimmigrant status,” Etter wrote.
DHS did not immediately respond to a comment request about Garces Perez’s petition to be released and his intent to seek a visa.

The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization that is funded in part by donations from members, foundations and corporate sponsors. sources.news_title: ICE Shooting of Austin Delivery Driver in His Back Sparks Protests and Calls for Shutting Down ICE
sources.text:
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was working as a delivery driver in North Austin on Sunday when an encounter with federal immigration officers ended in gunfire. An ICE officer shot the 28-year-old Venezuelan national on September 20, leaving him seriously wounded. He was later discharged from the hospital into ICE custody.
The shooting happened near Research Boulevard and Anderson Square during an immigration operation. Reuters reported that a brief foot pursuit preceded the gunfire. Local accounts have also raised questions about a collision involving an ICE vehicle and Perez’s car. Officials have yet to establish publicly the full sequence of events or why the officer fired. Although Perez was shot in the torso, authorities have not confirmed whether the shot entered from the front or back.
His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, disputes federal claims about his immigration status. ICE says Perez entered the country illegally and had a final order of removal; his legal team says he entered through a lawful parole process. His attorneys have also raised concerns about his medical care after he was transferred to a detention facility.
News of the shooting brought protesters to the area, where demonstrators chanted “Abolish ICE” and demanded answers. The gatherings continued into the night, with officers using crowd-control measures as tensions rose. Austin police say they did not take part in the federal operation.
Mayor Kirk Watson has called for Austin police and the Texas Rangers to have a role in investigating the shooting. Federal authorities say Homeland Security Investigations is examining the incident with FBI assistance. For local leaders, the question is whether that process will provide the independence and public accounting needed to establish what happened.
The case lands amid broader scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement after fatal shootings involving U.S. citizens, including Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. Their deaths have intensified demands for footage, records and outside review when agents use deadly force. In Austin, those demands now center on Perez, the circumstances of the pursuit and the decision to shoot a man who survived but remains in federal custody.

sources.news_title: Family of delivery driver shot in Austin ICE encounter demanding answers: Lawyer
sources.text:
The man was a Venezuelan national in the country illegally, according to DHS.
A Venezuelan migrant who was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer in Austin, Texas, spoke out on Monday from a federal detention facility, saying he is in a lot of pain and still has a bullet lodged near his spine.
The shooting on Sunday of 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez has prompted protests and backlash from local officials.
Garces Perez was delivering for DoorDash at the time of the encounter with ICE, his lawyer and the delivery platform confirmed to ABC News.
During a news conference Monday afternoon, his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said she was able to speak to Garces Perez after previously not being told of his whereabouts. She said that he was taken to Pearsall detention facility 130 miles from Austin around 4 a.m. on Monday.
Garces Perez's wife, Elizdar, stood next to Lincoln-Goldfinch during the news conference as the attorney recounted what Garces Perez told her.
During the news conference, Garces Perez called in and gave his version of what occurred during Sunday's incident.
"I am not doing well due to the gunshot wound, and I have not received the medical attention that I require," Garces Perez said in Spanish through an interpreter.
He said he is "in a lot of pain" and that doctors left a bullet inside his body "because it was close to his spine."
He said the encounter with the ICE officers unfolded as he was making a DoorDash delivery.
"An SUV rode next to him and tried to hit him," he said through the interpreter. "He thought it was like an aggressive driver. Turns out it was not. He asked the ICE officer if he could please pull over so that they could detain him. They said ‘no’ and they side-swiped him. He did a U-Turn to try and find a spot to park so that he could go with them and they basically ran into him and then shot him."
He said the ICE officers never asked him to stop or turned on their lights and siren.
"The only time they turned on any lights or sirens was after they side-swiped him and like, hit him."
Garces Perez said he still doesn't know how many times he was shot, and added that he felt one of the bullets hit him. He alleged that the ICE officers did not immediately attend to his injuries.
"One of the officers got into my car and forcibly turned it off. I told him I was in a lot of pain and I thought I was going to pass out. And then the EMTs arrived and that was that," Garces Perez said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch noted that an initial statement from the Department of Homeland Security said that Garces Perez was shot during a foot chase. But Garces Perez said that is inaccurate.
"There was no foot chase," he said, adding that he "never got out of the vehicle until he had to get out of the vehicle."
The Department of Homeland Security issued a statement on social media Sunday, saying, "Homeland Security Investigations, with the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, is leading the investigation into the officer involved shooting of an illegal alien from Venezuela, who illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal, during a law enforcement operation today in Austin, TX."
"The illegal alien’s condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal," the statement added. "This is a developing situation, and we will update the public when more information becomes available."
Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a post on X that her client was in the country legally and had applied for asylum.
ABC News has reached out to ICE for additional comment.
Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said in a statement he is "very angry and extremely disappointed that a person was shot on the streets of Austin by ICE."
"While I’m angry and disappointed, I’m not surprised. This has happened in other cities. With the rogue nature of ICE and the chaos we’re seeing fomented by ICE, there’s no reason to be surprised. Austinites have a right to know what happened and they have a right to feel safe in their community," he wrote on X.
A video obtained by ABC News shows the moments after Garces Perez was shot. Taken by a witness and provided to a local city councilmember, the video shows him sitting hunched over in the driver's seat of a blue sedan as ICE officers surround the car.
The man can be heard saying in Spanish that he was shot because he did not "brake." Later in the video, the man is seen handcuffed while officers cut his shirt, exposing a gunshot wound on his back.
ICE officials were conducting license plate checks to carry out their enforcement operations when they had a positive match on the vehicle registered to Garces Perez, who had an order to be deported, a law enforcement source also told ABC News.
The Department of Homeland Security has not given a full accounting of what occurred on Sunday and has not said whether the officers were wearing body-worn cameras during the incident.
An Austin city councilmember told ABC News that city police were not permitted to conduct a crime scene investigation.
"The crime scene was entirely controlled by ICE ... HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, as well as state police, Department of Public Safety, and so the city police were not being permitted to conduct a crime scene investigation,” Austin Councilmember Mike Siegel told ABC News.
The councilmember told ABC News that he is working with city officials to ensure that the ICE officer who allegedly shot the individual is not allowed to leave Texas.
ABC News' Armando Garcia contributed to this report.

sources.text:
Austin officials are demanding an independent role in the investigation of a shooting by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer that left a Venezuelan delivery driver hospitalized Sunday, setting up the latest confrontation between local authorities and federal immigration agencies over who examines the conduct of agents who open fire.
The man, identified by his lawyers as 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, was shot once in the torso on the city's north side and was in serious but stable condition at a hospital, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said at a news conference alongside Mayor Kirk Watson and other city officials. Davis said Austin police were not involved in the federal operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop and what she described, on preliminary information, as a brief foot pursuit.
Garcés Perez was working as a DoorDash driver at the time of the encounter, his lawyer and the delivery platform confirmed. His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said he called his wife around 12:30 p.m. to tell her he had been shot, crying out in pain before the call cut off — the only information his family had for hours afterward.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not participate in the city's news conference. In a statement, the department confirmed the man was in stable condition and "in federal custody pending removal," saying he had entered the country under the previous administration and had a final order of removal. A senior administration official said Monday that Garcés Perez had no criminal history beyond his immigration status. Homeland Security Investigations, with FBI assistance, will lead the investigation into the shooting, the department said.
That arrangement is precisely what Austin officials are contesting. Watson, a Democrat, said he wants the city's police department involved to provide "clear, third-party eyes" on the process, arguing it would not be appropriate for ICE to investigate itself — a concern sharpened by the fact that Homeland Security Investigations is a component of ICE. Asked whether the city knows the whereabouts of the agent who fired, the mayor acknowledged it does not, adding that he hoped an officer involved in a shooting would not leave the city or the state.
The Travis County District Attorney's office went further, formally requesting that Austin police and county prosecutors be included as co-equal partners in the investigation and that the federal government grant access to the evidence, noting that the incident may have included violations of state law.
City Council Member Mike Siegel offered the most detailed public account of the shooting itself, saying he was told an ICE Ford Expedition rammed the side of a small Toyota sedan before an officer got out and fired through the rear passenger window — at least two shots, by his account. Siegel also said federal officers and state police prevented local police from conducting a crime scene investigation for several hours, and demanded that state or city authorities detain the officer to prevent what he called a flight from justice. Photographs from the scene showed a dark blue Toyota with what appeared to be bullet holes. Federal authorities have not described what led to the shooting or addressed those claims.
The shooting drew a crowd of roughly a hundred protesters to the scene, where demonstrators confronted police officers holding riot shields as passing cars honked in support. U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, an Austin Democrat, said the city has experienced a surge of ICE activity, particularly in the north-central area where the shooting occurred. "ICE needs to get out of our city and start telling people the truth," he said, while calling for the full facts of the case to be established.

Earlier this month, two American teenagers said they were assaulted by agents in Alamo after recording an immigration stop. Whether Austin's demands fare differently now rests on decisions in Washington. The district attorney's request for evidence access, the mayor's call for third-party involvement and the unanswered question of the agent's whereabouts all await a federal response — and until one comes, a wounded delivery driver in federal custody, a car with bullet holes and two irreconcilable institutional accounts are what the public record holds.

sources.news_title: ICE Shoots Man in Austin Doing Food Delivery, Spurring Protests
sources.text:
An immigration enforcement agent shot and injured a man in Austin on Sunday, city officials said.
Police nor the U.S. Department of Homeland Security identified the man. But Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, an Austin immigration lawyer, said she was hired to represent the man and that he was released from the hospital and into federal custody Sunday evening.
She identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, and said he had a valid work permit and entered the U.S. legally. The attorney said he was doing a DoorDash delivery when the shooting happened, and the man subsequently called his wife from inside the vehicle.
In a statement issued late Sunday night, DHS officials said Homeland Security Investigations — one of the department branches — would probe the shooting, with support from the FBI. Without naming Garces Perez, the statement said he entered the country illegally during the Biden administration but did not provide additional information.
Former President Joe Biden’s administration granted temporary immigration benefits to citizens from a number of countries who could not return home safely, including those from Venezuela. President Donald Trump’s administration has erased those protections and targeted those people.
DHS officials also said the shooting happened during a law enforcement operation but did not detail how the man came onto their radar. The department added that his condition has stabilized, before suggesting that federal authorities are seeking to deport him.
Dozens of protesters gathered at the site of the shooting throughout the day, angrily shouting at law enforcement officers after what was at least the third instance of an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shooting a person in Texas since March 2025. Austin’s mayor said the shooting came amid increased ICE operations in the city in the recent few weeks.
On Sunday afternoon, an ICE agent shot a man after a “small foot pursuit,” Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis and other city officials said during a news conference. The man was wounded by a single gunshot in the upper torso, local officials said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch said the family hadn’t “been permitted to see him and have not received a meaningful update regarding his current status or circumstances. Our immediate concern is ensuring that his family receives accurate and timely information and that appropriate access and communication are provided while the matter is being addressed.”
The scene of the shooting at times became intense. Dozens of Austin police officers were at the scene near Research Boulevard and Anderson Square. Just before 6 p.m., officers shot pepper ball-like projectiles at the crowd after some demonstrators threw rocks and water bottles at law enforcement as some were readying to leave the area.
Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said at a news conference earlier in the day that he wants an independent investigation into the shooting, in part, because of the “chaos” we see it causing.
Even though Austin police were not involved in the operation that led to the shooting, he said it is important that the city’s residents know what happened and why.
Watson said he is “angry” but “not surprised at all” that an ICE agent has shot someone in the city, especially since immigration operations have picked up in the past few weeks.
Austin police and Texas Rangers plan to investigate the shooting along with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the federal agency that oversees immigration enforcement, Davis said.
“If there’s nothing wrong with that, they should welcome an investigation. And if you’re pro law enforcement, you should see that an investigation that is done right will only enhance credibility,“ the mayor said. “Austinites should know the truth, and I am pleased that we’re in a situation where Austin will also be involved in this investigation.”
Officials from the Travis County District Attorney’s Office, led by José Garza, said they want to review the evidence Austin police gathers as part of its investigation.
“We further request cooperation from the federal government in giving us access to the evidence. As has occurred in other jurisdictions, it is possible that this incident included violations of state law,” the office’s statement reads.
Sheridan Nolen, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Public Safety, said state troopers received a call at around 12:50 p.m. from ICE officials asking for help in a pursuit of a blue Toyota Corolla. Before troopers arrived, the ICE agent had shot the man, Nolen said.
“Once they arrived, DPS Troopers immediately began assisting partner law enforcement agencies in performing medical treatment on the driver of the Toyota Corolla,” Nolen said.
Dozens of demonstrators remained at the North Austin scene into the evening, some carrying signs and flags, shouting expletives about ICE and police.
David Torres, 24, learned of the shooting through connections from a community group he runs, Dare to Struggle. He showed up about 2:30 p.m. and planned to stay as long as there was a crowd.
“As long as these deportations continue, more and more people will be tortured behind walls and killed on the streets,” he said.
Trump’s administration has increased its immigration enforcement operations across the country, including Texas, a state with one of the largest immigration populations. A quarter of the half of million migrants the Trump administration has arrested and seeking to deport are from Texas.
It’s unclear when or under what immigration program the man injured Sunday may have entered the country. But under the Biden administration, the DHS had created pathways for some immigrants, including Venezuelans, to enter the U.S. legally.
Many Venezuelans had entered the U.S. using the CBP One cellphone application that required people to make an appointment to meet an immigration official at a port of entry at the border. Others entered under a parole program for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans, which allowed people to apply from their home country. If they passed a criminal background check and could prove they would be financially stable they would be allowed to enter the U.S. Through either program, the person was allowed to apply for a work permit. Many Venezuelans who applied moved to Texas.
On his first day back in office, President Trump scrapped the programs and classified migrants in those programs as “illegal aliens” as part of his mass deportation efforts. Advocacy groups have sued the Trump administration over the moves arguing that the White House didn’t follow standard procedure to cancel the programs the right way and that the Biden administration had the legal right to parole immigrants into the country as stated in immigration law. The lawsuits are pending.
The administration’s increased immigration enforcement has led to ICE agents fatally shooting other people across the country, including in Texas. The enforcement has also led to deaths of immigrants in immigrant detention centers.
Immigration agents in January fatally shot 37-year-old Renée Good and 37-year-old Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during separate protests against immigration enforcement operations.
In March 2025, Ruben Ray Martinez, 23, was fatally shot by an ICE agent in South Padre Island after officers said he “bumped” them with his car. The death of Martinez, who was born and raised in San Antonio, is the first known killing of an American by immigration agents under Trump’s second administration.
This summer, an ICE officer fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 7. His family said Araujo was on his way to work and may have feared he was being robbed. Investigations into that killing are ongoing.
U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, who also at Sunday’s news conference, said he supported outside agencies investigating the shooting because “ICE has not been truthful in shootings in other cities.”
“It is appropriate for this community to ask for independence, to ask for transparency, and to ask for accountability,” he said. “This is a pattern. It’s a disturbing pattern, and it’s got to stop.”

The man was taken to a local hospital and was “in serious but stable condition” after being shot in the torso, Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz said at a news conference earlier.
The White House referred NBC News to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. A spokesperson for the DHS, the federal agency to which Immigration and Customs Enforcement belongs, said in a statement late Sunday that the man was stable and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S.
Immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch identified him as Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, 28, and said he was an asylum seeker who entered the country through a parole program.
“Today at 12:30, Wilber called his wife to tell her that he had been shot,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said in an interview. “And he was yelling in agony, and the call cut off. That was all she knew.”

“Once they arrived, DPS Troopers immediately began assisting partner law enforcement agencies in performing medical treatment on the driver of the Toyota Corolla,” she said in a statement.

“Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened. We can see the lies with our own eyes. We will demand truth, transparency and accountability,” he said in a post on X.

The Briefing:
- An ICE agent shot 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in the torso during a Sunday DoorDash run in North Austin, and he was released from the hospital straight into federal custody hours later, before his family could learn where he'd been taken.
- Three different accounts exist for what happened right before the shots — a possible foot chase, a car boxed in from behind, and a vehicle pursuit state troopers hadn't yet reached — and no video or body-camera footage has been released to settle it.
- It's at least the third ICE-linked shooting of a person in Texas since March 2025, part of a wider national count that puts the number of people shot by ICE and CBP agents under the second Trump administration at roughly 20, with a July congressional letter putting an earlier figure at 22 shootings and six deaths.
A federal immigration agent shot and wounded a DoorDash driver in North Austin on Sunday afternoon, then released him from the hospital directly into ICE custody before his family could find out where he'd gone. The case, confirmed by CNN and NBC News, is already being weighed against a string of earlier ICE shootings that local and federal officials describe very differently.
Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan national, was mid-delivery when the shooting happened just before 1 p.m. at the intersection of U.S. 183 and Anderson Square, according to CNN. Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz said he took a single gunshot wound to the torso and was rushed to Dell Seton Medical Center in serious but stable condition, per the Austin American-Statesman. DoorDash confirmed to CNN that he was actively working a delivery at the time.
Three Versions of What Came First
Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis told reporters a foot pursuit may have preceded the shooting, while cautioning that her department hadn't yet been briefed by federal agents, per the Statesman. His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, described a different scene on Instagram: agents boxing in his car and firing through the rear window. A third account comes from the Texas Department of Public Safety, which told NBC News its troopers were called in to help ICE with a pursuit of a blue Toyota Corolla — but that the shooting had already happened by the time they arrived. No agency has released video or body-camera footage that would confirm any single version.
Hours after the shooting, DHS posted on X that Garcés Pérez had entered the country illegally under the Biden administration and carried a final removal order, adding that "the illegal alien's condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal". Lincoln-Goldfinch rejects that account: she told the Texas Tribune that he held a valid work permit and had entered the U.S. lawfully, and his wife has said she was never aware of a removal order. Neither side has produced documentation, so both versions remain unverified claims rather than settled fact.
Six Hours in the Dark
Garcés Pérez's wife arrived at the hospital around 12:30 p.m. and was later told by staff that he wasn't there and asked to leave, Lincoln-Goldfinch has said. He wasn't discharged until roughly 4:30 p.m., moved directly into what his attorney called ICE custody, and his family still didn't know where he'd been taken by that evening. "We are deeply concerned that his wife and family have not been permitted to see him," Lincoln-Goldfinch said, per NBC News.
Officials Say They've Watched This Before
Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said the shooting didn't surprise him, citing what he described as ICE's aggressive tactics in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis. "While I'm unhappy and I'm angry about it, I'm not surprised at all," he said, according to CNN. The two fatal shootings most frequently invoked in that comparison — of U.S. citizens Renée Good and Alex Pretti — both happened in Minneapolis in January, 17 days apart, during a federal enforcement surge there, per CBS Minnesota.
Texas has its own recent record. In July, an ICE officer fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old father of three, during a stop of his work van near Houston; DHS said he tried to ram an agent's vehicle, a claim the men riding with him have disputed and that remains unproven, according to CNN. Six days later, an ICE officer in Biddeford, Maine, killed 25-year-old Colombian delivery driver Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero after his car was struck by an agency vehicle, per the Washington Post. Sunday's shooting is at least the third tied to ICE in Texas alone since March 2025, when a Homeland Security Investigations agent fatally shot 23-year-old U.S. citizen Ruben Ray Martinez in South Padre Island — a case that didn't surface publicly for nearly a year, as NPR has reported.
A National Count That Keeps Moving
A running CNN tracker puts the number of people shot by on-duty ICE and CBP agents under the second Trump administration at roughly 20. That figure sits oddly against an earlier one: a July letter signed by 198 House Democrats cited 22 shootings and six deaths as of that month, according to The Hill — a higher tally from two months earlier than the more recent tracker shows. Neither source explains the gap, so it's presented here as an open discrepancy rather than a resolved one.
Homeland Security Investigations, working with the FBI, says it's leading the federal review of Sunday's shooting, though it had released no findings by Sunday night, per CNN. Rep. Greg Casar, whose district covers the shooting site, sent DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin a letter demanding a congressional briefing by Sept. 28 along with full body- and dash-camera footage. "Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened," Casar said, according to NPR.
The Travis County District Attorney's office is asking to be treated as a "co-equal partner in the investigation" rather than leaving the review to federal agents alone, per CNN. The League of United Latin American Citizens also weighed in, with national president Roman Palomares saying accountability shouldn't rest with the agency that did the shooting: "No agency should be the sole judge of its own conduct," according to a CNN report carried by Yahoo News. As of Sunday night, DHS had not said whether the agent involved was wearing a body camera.

Watson said he was not surprised by ICE’s involvement, given “the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days.”
Watson and other Texas Democrats have also called for independent investigations into the incident. James Talarico, who’s campaigning for a U.S. Senate seat, said he was “closely following” the reports and urged a probe that released available footage of the shooting. “Previous incidents have shown that this agency cannot be trusted to report all the facts,” Talarico said in a statement released to the media.
The District Attorney’s Office in Travis County, which includes Austin, requested to partner with city police in the investigation and for the federal government to cooperate in providing access to evidence. It added: “As has occurred in other jurisdictions, it is possible that this incident included violations of state law.”
Rep. Greg Casar (D, Texas) wrote a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and acting ICE director David Venturella seeking a congressional briefing on Sept. 28, and asked the agencies to publicly release all body and dash camera footage from federal officers present at the scene and recorded communications between agents before and after the shooting.
Casar and Watson claimed that ICE activity in Austin has increased in recent weeks amid President Donald Trump’s implementation of his strict anti-immigrant agenda. “It’s a disturbing pattern,” Casar said, “and it has got to stop.”
Here’s what we know so far.
What happened?
The shooting occurred near the intersection of Anderson Square and Research Boulevard in Austin. The Texas Tribune reported that Texas state troopers received a call at around 12:50 p.m. from ICE officials, citing Sheridan Nolen, a spokesperson for the state’s Department of Public Safety. The officials reportedly asked for help to pursue a blue Toyota Corolla.

They identified a man who sustained a gunshot wound to the torso, with Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis adding that preliminary information pointed to a “small foot pursuit” happening before the shooting.
Authorities then added that the man was transferred to the Dell Seton Medical Center in stable condition.
Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch is the Austin-based immigration lawyer representing the man who was shot and his wife. According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, the wife received a phone call on Sunday afternoon from her husband, who said that he had been shot before the line went dead.
She then went to the scene of the incident, the attorney said, but her husband had already been moved to the hospital.
In videos posted to her social media channels on Sunday evening, Lincoln-Goldfinch reported that she and the wife were subsequently barred from entering the hospital or learning about the condition of the man who was shot. They were later told that the man was already in ICE custody; he had been taken into custody four hours after he was shot, according to Lincoln-Goldfinch.

Lincoln-Goldfinch identified the man who was shot as a 28-year-old Venezuelan named Wilber Rafael Garces Perez.

US: Man wounded in Texas after being shot by ICE agent
September 21, 2026
A man has been hospitalized in Austin, Texas after being shot by an officer of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), local officials said Sunday.
Austin's Mayor Kirk Watson expressed his anger over the shooting, calling for the involvement of the local police in a "clear-eyed" investigation into the incident.
What do we know about the ICE shooting in Austin?
The man suffered one gunshot wound in his torso during a brief foot pursuit in the Texan capital's north side shortly before 1 pm local time, Austin officials said at a press briefing.
He is at a local hospital in a serious but stable condition, the officials said, adding that the information on the incident was "very preliminary."
City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said.
Who is the man wounded by ICE agent?
The officials did not name the man or release his age and nationality but an immigration lawyer, representing his family, identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan.
Attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch said in a video published on her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and had no final order to be removed from the country.
The Associated Press later cited Goldfinch as saying that she did not know his current immigration status.
There is yet to be a statement on the shooting from ICE or the Department of Homeland Security that oversees the immigration agency.
Meanwhile, a group of about 100 protesters gathered at the site of the shooting and demonstrated against ICE's actions.
The protest was held across the street from a blue Toyota Corolla which had damage to its passenger-side door, news agency Reuters reported citing local TV, as ICE agents stood nearby.
Austin Mayor rails against 'rogue' ICE, calls for independent probe
Sunday's shooting is the latest in a slew of incidents involving ICE, which has become the face of an immigration clampdown by US President Donald Trump's Republican administration.
Watson, a Democrat, told the media that the shooting occurred amid a "significant increase, almost overnight" of ICE operations in Austin.
"While I'm angry and disappointed, I'm not surprised. This has happened in other cities. With the rogue nature of ICE and the chaos we're seeing fomented by ICE, there's no reason to be surprised," the Austin mayor wrote on X.
He called for an independent investigation into the shooting, with the Austin Police Department (APD) having a role in the probe.
He said that the people of Austin had a "right to know what happened" and "a right to feel safe in their community".
"Though APD was not involved in the shooting, I believe that there needs to be an investigation that APD assures is clear-eyed, as complete as possible, and independent," Watson said.
He added that police chief Davis had deployed the APD's Special Investigation Unit at the scene, elaborating that the unit is the one responsible for probing Austin's officer-involved shootings.
Watson said that Davis has also asked the Texas Rangers to help out in the investigation.
'Horror has come to our doorstep,' says Congressman
On Sunday, US Representative Greg Casar — a Texas Democrat — called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.
He accused ICE of not being "truthful" in shooting in other cities.
"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," Casar said.
"A few weeks ago as we saw the ICE surge come ... I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot," he told the media.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), with assistance from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), is leading the investigation into the officer-involved shooting, according to DHS.
The man, identified as 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was shot in the torso and was initially reported to be in serious but stable condition. His attorney has disputed the federal government's account of his immigration status, saying Perez entered the US legally.
What Happened In Austin?
According to Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis, the ICE agent shot Perez during a brief pursuit on foot shortly before 1 pm local time. Police said the federal agent's identity was not immediately known and that local authorities had not been fully briefed by ICE, Reuters reported.
Perez was taken to a local hospital with a torso injury. AP reported that his lawyer said he had no known criminal history or removal order, although those claims had not been independently established by authorities at the time of reporting.
The circumstances surrounding the shooting remain under investigation. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security had not provided details when local officials addressed reporters.
Why Are Officials Calling For An Investigation?

Democrat Texas Congressman Joaquin Castro demanded body camera footage and full responsibility.
US Representative Greg Casar called for an independent investigation, evidence preservation, and transparency after the shooting.
Gina Hinojosa, Texas State Representative, also prayed for the ful recovery of the man. She further said, “I reaffirm Mayor Kirk Watson’s call for the ICE agent involved in the shooting to remain in Texas until a full investigation concludes.”
Protesters also gathered near the scene following the shooting.

ICE agent shoots and wounds Venezuelan migrant in Austin, sparking protests
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A Texas ICE agent shot and wounded a Venezuelan migrant who was reportedly in the country illegally on Sunday, sparking angry protests near the scene in Austin, according to local authorities and the man’s attorney.
The officer allegedly shot the migrant — who was identified by his lawyer as 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez — once in the torso shortly before 1 p.m. following a “small foot pursuit” on the city’s north side, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said at a media briefing.
The shooting, which happened under a highway overpass, left Garces Perez in serious but stable condition at a nearby hospital, according to Austin Mayor Kirk Watson.
The wounded man is an alleged illegal immigrant from Venezuela with a final order of removal, Department of Homeland Security sources told Fox News.
More details about what led up to the gunfire and the ICE operation were not immediately available. Local officials said all information they had was “extremely preliminary” and called for a full investigation into the shooting.
“The city of Austin deserves answers,” Davis said. “We’re going to get all those questions answered, and we’ll be as transparent as we can be.”
The Venezuelan national’s immigration attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, told the New York Times that she and the man’s wife have been blocked from seeing Garces-Perez and do not know if he is still at the hospital or has been moved into ICE custody elsewhere.

The controversial immigration agency has been involved in a number of fatal shootings this year.

sources.news_title: ICE officer shoots, wounds man in Austin; protesters demand probe
sources.text:
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, on Sunday during a brief foot pursuit, local officials said, as the incident drew protests and calls for an independent investigation.
The man, identified by immigration attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch as 28-year-old Venezuelan Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was shot once in the torso and remained in serious but stable condition at a hospital, officials said.
Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said the shooting happened after a traffic stop in northern Austin. She cautioned that information about the incident was still preliminary. Austin police were not involved in the shooting, although local investigators were at the scene.
Mayor Kirk Watson said he was “very angry and extremely disappointed” that a person had been shot by ICE in Austin, adding that the city had seen a “significant increase, almost overnight” in ICE operations.
Watson said he wanted Austin police and other local authorities involved in the investigation rather than leaving it solely to ICE.
“I will say, frankly, from my perspective, the credibility of ICE doing some form of investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate,” Watson said.
US Rep Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, had called for an independent investigation shortly after the shooting was reported. He later sent a letter to the Department of Homeland Security seeking an immediate, independent probe, the release of all footage from the shooting and accountability for any wrongdoing by the agent involved.
“The horror has come to our city: ICE has shot a person in Austin this morning,” Casar wrote on X, adding that he wanted “truth, transparency and accountability.”
The Travis County district attorney's office also asked for local police and prosecutors to participate in the investigation and requested access to evidence held by federal authorities.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately provide details about the shooting.
Goldfinch said she believed Garces Perez had no criminal history or final order of removal, although she later said she did not know his current immigration status.
The attorney said Garces Perez's family initially struggled to obtain information from the hospital. His wife was later informed that he had been released into ICE custody several hours after the shooting. ICE officer shoots, injures man in Austin, officials say
The shooting in Austin, which injured Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, came more than two months after an ICE officer fatally shot a man in Houston.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in North Austin after a person was shot earlier on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Lujan/The Texas Tribune)
An immigration enforcement agent shot and injured a man in Austin on Sunday, city officials said.
Police nor the U.S. Department of Homeland Security identified the man. But Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, an Austin immigration lawyer, said she was hired to represent the man and that he was released from the hospital and into federal custody Sunday evening.
She identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, and said he had a valid work permit and entered the U.S. legally. The attorney said he was doing a DoorDash delivery when the shooting happened, and the man subsequently called his wife from inside the vehicle.
In a statement issued late Sunday night, DHS officials said Homeland Security Investigations — one of the department branches — would probe the shooting, with support from the FBI. Without naming Garces Perez, the statement said he entered the country illegally under Biden but did not provide additional information.
Former President Joe Biden’s administration granted temporary immigration benefits to citizens from a number of countries who could not return home safely, including those from Venezuela. President Donald Trump’s administration has erased those protections and targeted those people.
DHS officials also said the shooting happened during a law enforcement operation but did not detail how the man came onto their radar. The department added that his condition has stabilized, before suggesting that federal authorities are seeking to deport him.
Dozens of protesters gathered at the site of the shooting throughout the day, angrily shouting at law enforcement officers after what was at least the third instance of an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shooting a person in Texas since March 2025. Austin’s mayor said the shooting came amid increased ICE operations in the city in the recent few weeks.
On Sunday afternoon, an ICE agent shot a man after a “small foot pursuit,” Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis and other city officials said during a news conference. The man was wounded by a single gunshot in the upper torso, local officials said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch said the family hadn’t “been permitted to see him and have not received a meaningful update regarding his current status or circumstances. Our immediate concern is ensuring that his family receives accurate and timely information and that appropriate access and communication are provided while the matter is being addressed.”
The scene of the shooting at times became intense. Dozens of Austin police officers were at the scene near Research Boulevard and Anderson Square. Just before 6 p.m., officers shot pepper ball-like projectiles at the crowd after some demonstrators threw rocks and water bottles at law enforcement as some were readying to leave the area.
Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said at a news conference earlier in the day that he wants an independent investigation into the shooting, in part, because of the “chaos” we see it causing.
Even though Austin police were not involved in the operation that led to the shooting, he said it is important that the city’s residents know what happened and why.
Watson said he is “angry” but “not surprised at all” that an ICE agent has shot someone in the city, especially since immigration operations have picked up in the past few weeks.
Austin police and Texas Rangers plan to investigate the shooting along with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the federal agency that oversees immigration enforcement, Davis said.
“If there’s nothing wrong with that, they should welcome an investigation. And if you’re pro law enforcement, you should see that an investigation that is done right will only enhance credibility,“ the mayor said. “Austinites should know the truth, and I am pleased that we’re in a situation where Austin will also be involved in this investigation.”
Officials from the Travis County District Attorney’s Office, led by José Garza, said they want to review the evidence Austin police gathers as part of its investigation.
“We further request cooperation from the federal government in giving us access to the evidence. As has occurred in other jurisdictions, it is possible that this incident included violations of state law,” the office’s statement reads.
Sheridan Nolen, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Public Safety, said state troopers received a call at around 12:50 p.m. from ICE officials asking for help in a pursuit of a blue Toyota Corolla. Before troopers arrived, the ICE agent had shot the man, Nolen said.
“Once they arrived, DPS Troopers immediately began assisting partner law enforcement agencies in performing medical treatment on the driver of the Toyota Corolla,” Nolen said.
Dozens of demonstrators remained at the North Austin scene into the evening, some carrying signs and flags, shouting expletives about ICE and police.
David Torres, 24, learned of the shooting through connections from a community group he runs, Dare to Struggle. He showed up about 2:30 p.m. and planned to stay as long as there was a crowd.
“As long as these deportations continue, more and more people will be tortured behind walls and killed on the streets,” he said.
Trump’s administration has increased its immigration enforcement operations across the country, including Texas, a state with one of the largest immigration populations. A quarter of the half of million migrants the Trump administration has arrested and seeking to deport are from Texas.
It’s unclear when or under what immigration program the man injured Sunday may have entered the country. But under the Biden administration, the DHS had created pathways for some immigrants, including Venezuelans, to enter the U.S. legally.
Many Venezuelans had entered the U.S. using the CBP One cellphone application that required people to make an appointment to meet an immigration official at a port of entry at the border. Others entered under a parole program for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans, which allowed people to apply from their home country. If they passed a criminal background check and could prove they would be financially stable they would be allowed to enter the U.S. Through either program, the person was allowed to apply for a work permit. Many Venezuelans who applied moved to Texas.
On his first day back in office, President Trump scrapped the programs and classified migrants in those programs as “illegal aliens” as part of his mass deportation efforts. Advocacy groups have sued the Trump administration over the moves arguing that the White House didn’t follow standard procedure to cancel the programs the right way and that the Biden administration had the legal right to parole immigrants into the country as stated in immigration law. The lawsuits are pending.
The administration’s increased immigration enforcement has led to ICE agents fatally shooting other people across the country, including in Texas. The enforcement has also led to deaths of immigrants in immigrant detention centers.
Immigration agents in January fatally shot 37-year-old Renée Good and 37-year-old Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during separate protests against immigration enforcement operations.
In March 2025, Ruben Ray Martinez, 23, was fatally shot by an ICE agent in South Padre Island after officers said he “bumped” them with his car. The death of Martinez, who was born and raised in San Antonio, is the first known killing of an American by immigration agents under Trump’s second administration.
This summer, an ICE officer fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 7. His family said Araujo was on his way to work and may have feared he was being robbed. Investigations into that killing are ongoing.
U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, who also at Sunday’s news conference, said he supported outside agencies investigating the shooting because “ICE has not been truthful in shootings in other cities.”
“It is appropriate for this community to ask for independence, to ask for transparency, and to ask for accountability,” he said. “This is a pattern. It’s a disturbing pattern, and it’s got to stop.”

“I am not doing well due to the gunshot wound and I have not received the medical attention that I require,” Garces Perez said in Spanish. Lincoln-Goldfinch and other organizers provided an English translation as he was speaking.
Garces Perez also gave his account of how the shooting unfolded. He said an unarmed black SUV tried to sideswipe his car. When he realized that ICE agents were the drivers, he made a U-turn under a highway bridge so that he could park and they could safely pull him over. Instead, he said, they sideswiped him again, exited their car and shot him in the back of the neck. He said he’s not sure how many times the agents shot but is aware of one bullet wound.
KUT News spoke to two people who work at a business near the scene of the shooting, which occurred by the intersection U.S. 183 and Anderson Square. They said they heard two gunshots and went to see what happened.

A blue car with damage to its passenger-side door was seen at the scene of a shooting by an ICE agent in North Austin on Sunday afternoon.

“They shot you just to shoot you?” someone asks the man in the video.
“They shot me because I didn’t stop,” he responds.
ICE agents, including one whose face is covered by a black cloth, and an Austin police officer are standing next to the car. Asked if an ambulance is on the way, one of the officers answers, “yes.”

During the press conference, Garces Perez told reporters he didn’t receive any medical attention at Dell Seton. A protest forms at the scene of a ICE shooting at the intersection of Anderson Square and Research Boulevard.

ICE agents, including one whose face is covered by a black cloth, and an Austin police officer are standing next to the car. Asked if an ambulance is on the way, one of the officers answers, "yes."
Garces Perez was taken to Dell Seton Medical Center in stable condition, according to city officials. Lincoln-Goldfinch said he is now being held at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, roughly 130 miles southwest of Austin.
During the press conference, Garces Perez told reporters he didn't receive any medical attention at Dell Seton. When he asked if the bullet would be removed, he said, the doctor told him "they're in a hurry to get you out of here." He later slept on the floor of the detention center in Pearsall, still in pain, he said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch added that security staff at Dell Seton initially claimed Garces Perez wasn't there at all, and forced her and his wife to leave the premises. An attorney for the hospital later called Lincoln-Goldfinch and said Garces Perez had been released to ICE, she said.
In the hours after the shooting, protesters gathered at the scene and police used chemical agents to disperse the crowd. Police left the scene around 6 p.m., but protesters remained, moving construction materials at the intersection of Research Boulevard and Anderson Square to block a large portion of the road from incoming traffic.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said on X late Sunday that ICE is investigating the shooting with assistance from the FBI. The agency identified the shooting victim as a man from Venezuela "who illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal."
Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garces Perez came to the U.S. two years ago using the "CBP One" mobile app, which the Biden administration created to allow migrants seeking asylum to virtually schedule their appointments at an official port of entry. The government stopped using it after President Trump took office in 2025.
According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garces Perez also had a valid work permit. She said he missed a court hearing for his immigration case because he had moved, and the notice of the hearing was sent to his old address. That's what led to his final order of removal, or deportation order, she said.
Homeland Security Investigations, with the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, is leading the investigation into the officer involved shooting of an illegal alien from Venezuela, who illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order…
— Homeland Security (@DHSgov) September 21, 2026
Local officials call for transparency, preservation of evidence
At a City Hall news conference on Sunday, Austin Mayor Kirk Watson was quick to stress that Austin Police were not involved in the shooting. He added that he was "angry" about the shooting, but was not surprised, given how "ICE is doing its business these days."
Watson said he wanted APD to be involved in the investigation of the shooting to offer a "clear-eyed, third-party look" at what happened.
"This has happened in the city of Austin, the city of Austin deserves answers on what occurred. ... We're going to get all those questions answered and we're going to be as transparent as we can be," Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said.
U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, sent a letter to DHS calling for an independent investigation and accountability for the officer involved in the shooting.
"The agent must be suspended and remain in Austin while the investigation into the shooting is ongoing," he said.
He also requested that the federal government release unedited footage of the shooting, preserve and share evidence with state and local law enforcement, and give him and other members of Congress a briefing by Monday, Sept. 28, on whether ICE followed protocol during the shooting.
During the news conference Monday, Casar also demanded that ICE release Garces Perez. If he is deported, Casar warned the government would be removing a "key witness to this shooting."
"I don't care if you're a Democrat or Republican, we all believe the federal government should not be allowed to shoot you and then disappear you from the country so that no one can be held responsible," he said.
The shooting in Austin follows a string of such incidents across the country. Less than three months ago, ICE fatally shot two people within the span of one week, including Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston.
This is a developing story.

Casar, Castro call for probe, bodycam release after reported ICE shooting in Austin
AUSTIN - The report of an ICE shooting in Austin drew a sharp response Sunday from U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, who called for an independent investigation and the release of body camera footage.
“The horror has come to our city: ICE has shot a person in Austin this morning,” Casar said in a statement released Sunday.
“As the facts emerge, I am demanding a full, independent investigation, immediate release of the body camera footage, and accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law,” he said.
RELATED | Federal immigration officer shoots, injures man in Austin, report says
Casar also accused the agency of dishonesty in past shootings, saying, “Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened. We can see the lies with our own eyes.”
He said he expects community members to respond peacefully, adding, “Just like Americans have from Minneapolis to Houston, Austinites will speak out peacefully against this deadly mass deportation machine.”
Casar ended his statement by criticizing ICE’s actions nationally: “ICE has been terrorizing our country for far too long. We will not be silent.”
Rep. Joaquin Castro also addressed the incident, calling for the immediate release of body camera footage.
James Talarico has also made a statement regarding the shooting, saying that he and his campaign are following the incident closely.
I am closely following reports of a shooting involving federal immigration officials in Austin," said Talarico in a satement. "Previous incidents have shown that this agency cannot be trusted to report all the facts. We need a full, independent investigation that includes the release of any and all available footage. As we seek further information, my prayers are with those impacted and with the Austin community.
The Bexar County Democrats also released a statement in the aftermath of the shooting, condemning the shooting and demanding accountability.
Enough is enough," said Texas House Democratic Campaign Committee Chair Christina Morales. "ICE has repeatedly been overly aggressive and violent, due to a lack of training and accountability. There must be a full investigation into ICE's lawlessness. We demand answers.
